trial_name: SAHaRA — Liberal vs Restrictive Transfusion in Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (2025)
citation: English SW, Delaney A, Fergusson DA, Chassé M, Turgeon AF, Lauzier F, et al.; SAHARA Trial Investigators on behalf of the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group. Liberal or Restrictive Transfusion Strategy in Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(11):1079-1088.
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, open-label, pragmatic, blinded outcome adjudication
one_liner: In anaemic aSAH patients, a liberal transfusion threshold (10 g/dL) did not improve 12-month disability compared with a restrictive threshold (8 g/dL), despite reducing radiographic vasospasm.

pico.population: Adults with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage and hemoglobin ≤10.0 g/dL within 10 days of admission
pico.intervention: Liberal red-cell transfusion strategy (transfuse when Hb ≤10.0 g/dL)
pico.comparison: Restrictive red-cell transfusion strategy (transfuse only when Hb ≤8.0 g/dL)
pico.outcome: Unfavourable neurological outcome at 12 months (modified Rankin Scale ≥4)

background.existing_knowledge: Anaemia is common in aSAH due to phlebotomy, inflammation, haemodilution, operative blood loss, and critical illness. Red-cell transfusion is used to augment oxygen delivery but carries risks. Prior evidence was observational and small mechanistic studies, leaving equipoise on whether higher haemoglobin improves neurological outcomes.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether a liberal transfusion strategy improves patient-centred neurological outcomes in aSAH.
background.hypothesis: A liberal transfusion strategy (threshold 10.0 g/dL) would reduce unfavourable neurological outcome at 12 months compared with a restrictive strategy (threshold 8.0 g/dL).

methods.design: Pragmatic, investigator-initiated, open-label, randomised controlled trial with blinded outcome and imaging adjudication; conducted at 23 centres (Canada, Australia, USA); pilot phase (Oct 2015–Nov 2016) followed by full trial phase (Mar 2018–Jul 2023).
methods.setting: 23 centres in Canada, Australia, and USA.

inclusion: Adults (≥18 years) with first-ever aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage and haemoglobin ≤10.0 g/dL within the first 10 days after hospital admission.
exclusion: Contraindications to transfusion or known objection to receiving blood products.

methods.intervention: Liberal strategy: leukoreduced red-cell transfusion mandatory when haemoglobin ≤10.0 g/dL; transfused 1 unit at a time; protocol applied from randomisation until 21 days after hospital presentation, death, or discharge (whichever came first). Daily haemoglobin monitoring to at least day 10 or ICU discharge.
methods.comparison: Restrictive strategy: leukoreduced red-cell transfusion permitted only when haemoglobin ≤8.0 g/dL; 1 unit at a time; same intervention window and monitoring.
methods.blinding: Open-label treatment allocation; blinded assessment of primary 12-month mRS outcome; blinded adjudication of radiographic/clinical secondary brain injury outcomes.
methods.sample_size_power: Power calculation: 740 patients to detect a 25% relative reduction in unfavourable neurological outcome (mRS ≥4) from 40% to 30% with 80% power at two-sided 5% significance level, allowing ~3% loss to follow-up.
methods.primary_outcome: Unfavourable neurological outcome at 12 months (modified Rankin Scale ≥4).
secondary_outcomes: EQ-5D visual analogue scale at 12 months
New radiographic vasospasm during intervention period
New delayed cerebral ischaemia during intervention period
New cerebral infarction during intervention period
Any red-cell transfusion during intervention period
Red-cell units transfused during intervention period
methods.follow_up: Primary endpoint at 12 months post-randomisation; in-hospital secondary outcomes assessed during intervention window (up to day 21 after presentation) with follow-up for key in-hospital events up to 28 days where specified.

headline_bullets: The liberal strategy did not significantly reduce the primary endpoint (mRS ≥4 at 12 months): RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.09; P=0.22.
Despite a reduction in radiographic vasospasm (RR 0.77; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.95), there was no clear signal for delayed cerebral ischaemia, infarction, or mortality.
Protocol separation was substantial: 99.7% of liberal-strategy patients received transfusion vs 35.0% in the restrictive group (RR 2.86; 95% CI 2.42 to 3.38), with a median of 2 vs 0 red-cell units.

outcomes_table.outcome: Primary: unfavourable neurological outcome at 12 months (mRS ≥4)
outcomes_table.note: Primary analysis adjusted for centre and sex; outcome data available for 725/732 (99.0%) analysed participants.
Not powered for mortality; CI includes clinically important benefit and no effect.
Higher score indicates better functional independence.

outcomes_table.outcome: Quality of life: EQ‑5D visual analogue scale at 12 months
New radiographic vasospasm during intervention period
outcomes_table.note: Radiographic outcome adjudicated by a blinded assessor; fewer cases with liberal strategy.

outcomes_table.outcome: New delayed cerebral ischaemia during intervention period
outcomes_table.note: No clear effect; CI includes benefit and no effect.

outcomes_table.outcome: New cerebral infarction during intervention period
outcomes_table.note: No clear effect on infarction despite lower radiographic vasospasm.

outcomes_table.outcome: Tertiary (implementation): any red-cell transfusion during intervention period
outcomes_table.note: Marked separation in exposure to transfusion.

outcomes_table.outcome: Tertiary (dose): red-cell units transfused during intervention period
outcomes_table.note: Substantial increase in cumulative donor exposure with liberal strategy.
Open-label outcome; no separation in ventilation duration or length of stay.
Events were rare; wide confidence interval.

safety: Acute transfusion reaction: 2/366 (0.5%) in liberal vs 1/366 (0.3%) in restrictive; OR 2.01 (95% CI 0.18 to 22.3).

domains.notes: Central, concealed, computer-generated randomisation with variable block sizes (4 and 6) stratified by centre; minimises selection bias.
742 patients randomised; 10 excluded post-randomisation due to withdrawn/declined consent or removal of data; primary outcome available for 725/732 (99.0%) analysed patients.
Open-label treatment; primary endpoint (mRS) and imaging endpoints assessed by blinded adjudicators, reducing detection bias.

Overall protocol violations infrequent (12 violations affecting 11 patients, 1.5%); but protocol deviations common in implementation metrics (e.g., time-to-transfusion >6 hours in 134 liberal patients).
Groups well balanced; median haemoglobin at randomisation 9.4 g/dL (IQR 9.0–9.7) in both groups.
Radiographic vasospasm before randomisation in 36.6% (liberal) vs 35.0% (restrictive); DCI before randomisation in 13.7% vs 15.6%.
Randomisation median 3 days after admission (IQR 2–5); intervention window median 17 days (liberal) vs 16 days (restrictive).
Median pretransfusion haemoglobin 9.6 g/dL (liberal) vs 7.6 g/dL (restrictive); any transfusion 99.7% vs 35.0%; median units 2 vs 0.
Protocol deviations: early transfusion near restrictive threshold in 8 restrictive patients; missed transfusion when Hb 9.5–10.0 in 33 liberal patients; separation remained large.
Use of common aSAH co-interventions broadly similar between groups.
Primary and key imaging outcomes prespecified with blinded adjudication; non-blinded tertiary outcomes vulnerable to performance bias.
Prespecified ITT analysis with mixed models and adjustment for centre/sex; prespecified interim analysis with conservative stopping boundary; no multiplicity correction for secondary outcomes.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity appears moderate-to-strong given concealed randomisation, high follow-up completeness, and blinded adjudication for key endpoints, tempered by unavoidable open-label delivery and frequent implementation deviations (particularly transfusion timing) that could dilute or complicate estimation of small treatment effects.

domains.notes: Adults with aSAH and clinically relevant anaemia (≤10.0 g/dL) cared for in contemporary, high-resource neurocritical care systems; median age 56 years; substantial burden of high-grade haemorrhage (Modified Fisher grade 3–4 majority) and severe clinical grade (WFNS IV–V ~one-third).

Multinational (Canada, Australia, USA) tertiary centres with ready access to daily haemoglobin monitoring, leukoreduced blood products, aneurysm securing, CSF diversion, and vasospasm surveillance/treatment.
Findings may not generalise to non-aneurysmal SAH, patients with major active haemodynamic bleeding, those who refuse transfusion, or settings where blood supply/monitoring differs materially.

The strategy is operationally simple (threshold-based transfusion) and aligns with routine ICU workflows, but observed delays to transfusion highlight that real-world effectiveness depends on implementation fidelity.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate to similar high-income neurocritical care systems managing aSAH with frequent anaemia, but may be limited where blood product availability, monitoring cadence, or standard vasospasm/DCI management differs substantially.

strengths: Largest pragmatic randomised evaluation of transfusion thresholds in aSAH to date, addressing an important practice-variation question.
Multicentre, multinational design (23 centres) with concealed randomisation and high completeness of 12‑month follow-up.
Blinded adjudication of the primary functional endpoint and key imaging-based secondary outcomes.
Large achieved separation in haemoglobin at transfusion and transfusion exposure, supporting a biologically meaningful contrast.
limitations: Open-label delivery may bias clinician-driven outcomes and co-interventions (particularly tertiary outcomes such as intubation).
Notable proportion had vasospasm/DCI already present before randomisation, potentially limiting modifiability of downstream injury.
Implementation deviations (especially transfusion timing) were common and could attenuate differences attributable to the intended thresholds.
Secondary outcomes were not multiplicity-adjusted; signals outside the primary endpoint should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.

critical_appraisal.summary: SAHARA is a well-conducted, pragmatic RCT that provides high-quality evidence that a liberal transfusion strategy does not improve functional outcome in aSAH, despite reducing radiographic vasospasm. The open-label design and implementation deviations are limitations, but the primary outcome was blinded and follow-up was near-complete.
strengths: Largest pragmatic randomised evaluation of transfusion thresholds in aSAH to date, addressing an important practice-variation question.
Multicentre, multinational design (23 centres) with concealed randomisation and high completeness of 12‑month follow-up.
Blinded adjudication of the primary functional endpoint and key imaging-based secondary outcomes.
Large achieved separation in haemoglobin at transfusion and transfusion exposure, supporting a biologically meaningful contrast.
weaknesses: Open-label delivery may bias clinician-driven outcomes and co-interventions (particularly tertiary outcomes such as intubation).
Notable proportion had vasospasm/DCI already present before randomisation, potentially limiting modifiability of downstream injury.
Implementation deviations (especially transfusion timing) were common and could attenuate differences attributable to the intended thresholds.
Secondary outcomes were not multiplicity-adjusted; signals outside the primary endpoint should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.

sections.authors_conclusion: Overall, SAHARA argues against routine higher haemoglobin targets in aSAH, supporting restrictive thresholds unless individual clinical indications justify deviation.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: SAHARA provides high-quality, pragmatic randomised evidence that a liberal red-cell transfusion threshold (≥10 g/dL) in anaemic aSAH does not improve 12‑month disability compared with a restrictive threshold (≥8 g/dL), despite materially increasing transfusion exposure. The trial’s physiology-adjacent signal (less radiographic vasospasm) did not translate into fewer infarctions, DCI, or better function, reinforcing that patient-centred outcomes—not surrogates—should drive transfusion strategy selection in aSAH.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage and anaemia (Hb ≤10 g/dL) managed in high-resource neurocritical care settings.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That transfusion is harmful; rather, routine liberal transfusion does not improve functional outcome and increases donor exposure.
implementation_caveats: Individualised decisions may still be warranted for patients with ongoing cerebral ischaemia or other compelling indications.
Implementation fidelity (timely transfusion) is important if a liberal strategy is chosen.

controversies.notes: Earlier aSAH randomised evidence was limited in size and scope (e.g., a single-centre trial targeting higher haemoglobin goals), leaving uncertainty about patient-centred neurological benefit and the plausibility of meaningful effect sizes in aSAH.

The dissociation between improved radiographic vasospasm and unchanged infarction/DCI/12‑month function reinforces methodological caution about surrogate endpoints in aSAH and highlights the importance of long-term functional outcomes as primary endpoints; published commentary has emphasised this interpretive tension and the clinical costs of higher transfusion exposure.

SAHARA’s results align with a broader acute brain injury transfusion literature: the TRAIN trial (acute brain injury population) similarly did not demonstrate clear functional benefit with liberal thresholds compared with restrictive thresholds.

In traumatic brain injury, the HEMOTION trial found no improvement in neurological outcome with a liberal transfusion strategy (threshold 10 g/dL) compared with a restrictive strategy (threshold 7 g/dL), supporting the general direction of restrictive practice where specific indications are absent.

Contemporary general transfusion guidelines (AABB) recommend restrictive transfusion thresholds for most haemodynamically stable adults, and SAHARA provides high-quality aSAH-specific randomised evidence that is directionally consistent with these recommendations (while still allowing for individualised decisions in exceptional circumstances).

context_related_trials.relation: TRAIN trial (acute brain injury) also found no functional benefit with liberal transfusion.
HEMOTION trial (TBI) found no improvement in neurological outcome with liberal transfusion (threshold 10 g/dL) vs restrictive (7 g/dL).
AABB guidelines recommend restrictive transfusion thresholds for most haemodynamically stable adults, consistent with SAHARA.

unresolved_questions: Whether liberal transfusion benefits specific subgroups (e.g., those with severe vasospasm or delayed cerebral ischaemia) remains uncertain.
The optimal haemoglobin threshold for individual patients with ongoing ischaemia is not defined.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In anaemic aSAH, a liberal transfusion threshold (10 g/dL) does not improve 12-month functional outcome compared with a restrictive threshold (8 g/dL), despite reducing radiographic vasospasm, and increases transfusion exposure substantially.
